common_name: Violascens Bamboo (Violet-Flushed Hardy Running Timber Bamboo)
directions: This cold-hardy running timber bamboo is prized for shooting unusually early in spring and for the purplish-violet blush that appears on its new culms and sheaths before they mature to green. It grows into tall, fairly thin-walled canes that are harvested young for their tender, mild-flavored shoots in parts of China. Because it spreads aggressively by rhizome, confine it with a buried barrier or generous open ground, and thin congested culms periodically to keep the grove shooting well. It tolerates considerable winter cold once established, making it a reasonable choice where many timber bamboos struggle.

Fishscale bamboo gets its name from the overlapping, swollen sheath scars that ring each node, giving young canes a distinctive scaled texture unlike smoother Phyllostachys species. It forms dense, leafy groves of medium-height culms that work well as an informal screen or windbreak in a bamboo collection. As a running species it needs a barrier or isolated planting site to stay contained, and it tolerates a range of light conditions from fairly sunny to lightly shaded. Established groves are reliably cold hardy and need little care beyond periodic thinning of old culms.

common_name: Candy Cane Bamboo (Damarapa Striped Clumping Bamboo)
directions: Candy Cane bamboo is grown for its slender culms, which develop striking streaks of pink, yellow, and green along their length as they mature in good light, fading toward solid yellow-green with age. It forms a tight, non-invasive clump that works well as a specimen or container plant where its colorful canes can be seen up close. This Himalayan species is less cold hardy than many temperate bamboos, so it needs a sheltered spot and winter protection outside of mild climates. Give it consistent moisture and some shade from the hottest afternoon sun to keep foliage from scorching.

Blue Himalayan bamboo produces new culms coated in a striking powdery blue-white bloom that gradually wears off to reveal green canes beneath, making freshly emerged growth the main seasonal attraction. It is a true clumper with no running rhizomes, so it stays where planted and suits a sheltered courtyard or woodland-edge planting. Native to moist Himalayan forest margins, it prefers filtered light and shelter from strong wind and hard frost, performing best in mild, humid climates. Keep soil consistently moist and avoid exposed, open sites where winter cold or desiccating wind can damage the clump.

This is the higher-elevation Mexican subspecies most commonly sold in the ornamental trade, distinguished from typical Otatea acuminata by finer leaves, slightly shorter stature, and noticeably better cold tolerance. Thin, arching culms densely clothed in narrow leaves create the same graceful, fountain-like weeping effect the species is known for, making it a popular lawn specimen or softening accent near patios. It is a true clumping bamboo with no running rhizomes, tolerates heat and drought well once established, and handles brief light frosts better than the typical form. Full sun produces the densest, most upright growth, while some afternoon shade in the hottest climates keeps foliage from bleaching.

Silverstripe bamboo is a tropical clumping timber bamboo named for the conspicuous white-striped sheaths that wrap its young culms before falling away to reveal smooth green canes. It grows into a tall, dense, gracefully arching clump that is widely planted as a fast screen or windbreak in warm, humid regions such as South Florida. As a true clumper it does not send out invasive runners, but it is cold-tender and can be seriously damaged or killed by hard freezes, so it is only reliable in zones with mild winters. Give it full sun, warmth, and consistent moisture through its first year or two for the quickest establishment.

Pajuro, also called chachafruto or basul, is a fast-growing nitrogen-fixing tree from the mid-elevation Andes prized for its large flattened seeds, which are boiled or roasted and eaten like a starchy lima bean in Colombian and Ecuadorian soups and stews. The tree bears showy clusters of orange-red, hummingbird-pollinated flowers followed by long pods that each hold several thick seeds. It performs best in deep, well-drained soil within a cool-subtropical highland climate, since it favors the moderate year-round temperatures of 1,500-2,800 m Andean valleys over hot humid lowlands. Established trees tolerate pruning and are often grown as living fencing or shade for coffee while still producing an annual seed harvest.

subcategory: Brazilian Cerrado and restinga fruit tree
directions: Mangaba is a small, latex-bearing tree native to Brazil's sandy coastal restingas and Cerrado savanna, grown for its golf-ball-sized yellow fruit blushed with red, eaten fresh when fully soft or processed into pulp, juice, jam, and the ice cream popular across northeastern Brazil. The tree thrives in poor, fast-draining sandy soil and full sun, tolerating drought and heat better than most tropical fruit trees once established. Because flowers are self-incompatible, planting more than one seedling improves pollination and fruit set. Fruit ripens and drops quickly and bruises easily, so harvest fallen fruit daily rather than waiting to pick it from the tree.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Research and Education Center

subcategory: Brazilian Cerrado legume tree (edible nut and pulp)
directions: Baru is a deep-rooted legume tree of the Brazilian Cerrado savanna, grown for the woody pod enclosing a single almond-flavored kernel that is widely roasted and sold as a crunchy, protein-rich snack nut. The thick, fibrous pulp surrounding the hard pod is also sweet and edible, traditionally eaten fresh or fed to livestock and wildlife. Its extensive taproot makes baru exceptionally drought-tolerant once established, but trees are slow to bear and need many years of warm, frost-free growth before their first crop of pods. Give baru full sun and very well-drained, nutrient-poor soil, since it is adapted to seasonally dry savanna rather than wet tropical lowlands.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service National Plant Germplasm System

directions: This diminutive crested iris grows wild on brushy hillsides and woodland margins across Korea, sending up pale yellow flowers with a frilled crest on the falls just above a low fan of narrow leaves in mid-spring. It spreads gradually by creeping rhizomes to form a loose colony and prefers the same light shade, leaf-litter-rich soil, and even moisture found at its native forest-edge sites. Give it a spot that is not waterlogged in winter, since the shallow rhizomes are prone to rot in heavy, poorly drained ground. Divide congested patches after flowering if increase or rejuvenation is wanted.

Iris sanguinea is one of the wild beardless species behind the modern Siberian iris group, native to damp meadows and stream margins across Japan, Korea, and eastern Siberia. Slender, grassy foliage frames wiry stems carrying violet-blue flowers with narrow, veined falls in late spring, each stem typically holding two blooms. It tolerates both consistently moist soil and brief summer drying once established, making it adaptable to a border, pond margin, or naturalized meadow planting. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in early fall to keep flowering strong.

Ross's iris is a tiny beardless species found on dry, grassy mountain slopes across Korea and parts of Japan and China, forming tufts of narrow, grass-like leaves only a few inches tall. Solitary reddish-purple to violet flowers with a darker central stripe on the falls open close to the ground in very early spring, often before the foliage fully elongates. It is best suited to a rock garden, trough, or raised scree bed with sharp drainage, since it declines quickly in heavy or waterlogged soil. Give it a dry summer rest period similar to its native dry hillside habitat.

'Shogun' is a brightly variegated selection of the Japanese and Korean wild aster traditionally foraged as a spring green for yomena-gohan, here grown as an ornamental groundcover for its cream-margined foliage rather than for harvest. Lavender-blue daisy flowers appear in fall above spreading clumps of toothed leaves, extending interest well past the spring foliage display. It spreads at a moderate pace by rhizomes, making it useful as a woodland-edge groundcover or border filler, and tends to show the cleanest variegation with some direct morning sun. Divide congested clumps in spring every few years to maintain vigor and leaf color.

Known in Japan as fukujukusou, or 'flower of fortune and longevity,' this buttercup relative is traditionally displayed as a potted New Year's flower and is one of the earliest woodland bloomers, opening glossy golden-yellow cups often while frost or snow still lingers on the ground. After bloom, finely divided ferny foliage expands before the whole plant goes fully dormant and disappears by midsummer. It wants humus-rich, well-drained soil in the dappled light of deciduous shade, matching its native forest-floor habitat, and resents being disturbed once established. Established clumps slowly bulk up and are best left undivided for several years to build flowering size.

Known in Japan as senno, this traditional woodland-edge perennial carries clusters of brilliant orange-red flowers with notched, fringe-edged petals atop upright stems in mid to late summer. It grows naturally along the semi-shaded margins of satoyama woodland and thickets in Japan, Korea, and China, and performs best with morning sun followed by afternoon shade and consistently moist, humus-rich soil. The flower color is intense enough to anchor a partly shaded border or naturalized woodland-edge planting without appearing gaudy against green foliage. Stake taller stands in rich soil, since vigorous plants can lean after heavy rain.
